strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: continuous-time extrapolation of dynamic, renderable 3D scenes.
Combining persistent 3D Gaussian trajectories with a Transformer encoder and latent neural ODE is technically plausible and yields a clear two-stage framework.
The evaluation includes two established datasets, several relevant NeRF/3DGS baselines, deterministic and variational variants, and standard rendering metrics.
The reported improvements are substantial, particularly on NVFI, and the manuscript is generally understandable.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is insufficient to substantiate the main claims. There are no ablations for the ODE, Transformer, sequence-separation strategy, second-derivative regularizer, curriculum, or optional rendering loss, so the source of the gains is unknown.

The evaluation protocol is not specified precisely enough to establish a fair comparison. It is unclear whether baselines were retrained with exactly the same temporal splits and inputs, how hyperparameters were selected, and how stochastic variational predictions were converted into the single reported result. The test-time notation also inconsistently describes extrapolation timestamps as ending at t_max, previously defined as the observed boundary.

Claims of physically plausible, temporally smooth, long-term, arbitrary-time prediction are supported only by per-frame image metrics over 20–25% held-out horizons and one qualitative scene. There are no trajectory, acceleration, temporal-consistency, physics, irregular-time, or horizon-dependent evaluations.

The variational formulation is incomplete: the likelihood and its variance are undefined, uncertainty and multimodality are never evaluated, and sampling or aggregation at evaluation time is unexplained. Thus, the claimed advantage of probabilistic forecasting is unsupported.

Important implementation details are missing or inconsistent. The curriculum refers to a nonexistent section, the optional rendering loss is not formally defined, sequence sampling is vague, and handling of quaternion normalization and positive Gaussian scales is unspecified. There is also no code or resource statement.

The method appears to process each Gaussian trajectory independently, with no explicit spatial interaction or object-level coupling. The paper does not analyze this limitation or explain how coherent multi-object dynamics arise.
Despite emphasizing practical real-time rendering, the paper reports no training cost, inference latency, ODE function-evaluation count, memory use, Gaussian count, or rendering frame rate.

The qualitative evaluation is extremely limited and visually small. Several numerical statements are overstated—for example, ODE-GS is not consistently superior across all D-NeRF scenes—and no variance across seeds or statistical uncertainty is reported.

The conceptual novelty is moderate: the central contribution is primarily a combination of established deformable 3DGS, Transformer encoding, variational latent ODEs, and a standard smoothness penalty. Stronger validation is needed for this combination to be competitive at a top-tier venue.

The two-stage decomposition—first extracting Gaussian trajectories with a deformation model and then forecasting them with a latent ODE—is intuitive and technically plausible.
The evaluation includes two datasets, several relevant baselines, both deterministic and variational variants on D-NeRF, and standard rendering metrics.
The reported aggregate improvements are substantial, especially on NVFI, and would be noteworthy if supported by a more rigorous and reproducible evaluation.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is inadequate for the strength of the claims. There are no ablations for the latent ODE, Transformer, second-derivative regularizer, dynamic sequence separation, variational objective, or optional rendering loss. Consequently, it is impossible to determine which components produce the gains or whether an ordinary sequence predictor would perform similarly.

The extrapolation protocol is unclear and internally inconsistent. The problem formulation defines extrapolation as t > t_max, whereas the testing section says predictions are generated through t_max. The paper does not precisely identify which images and timestamps are available to Stage 1, how temporal splits interact with the original dataset splits, or how leakage from the interpolation model is prevented.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. There are no implementation details, hyperparameters, retraining protocols, or adaptation procedures for the baselines. Several baselines were designed primarily for interpolation, so directly extrapolating their time-conditioned fields may create a weak comparison. The very large gains therefore cannot be confidently attributed to the proposed method.

Despite claiming forecasting “far beyond” the training interval, the experiments report only averages over a short final 20–25% segment. There is no performance-versus-horizon analysis, evaluation at arbitrary intermediate times, or evidence about long-term stability.

The qualitative evaluation consists of only one small visualization from one D-NeRF scene and apparently one timestamp. This is far too limited to support claims of photorealism, temporal coherence, smoothness, or physically plausible motion; videos and results across diverse scenes and horizons are essential.

The variational motivation is not validated. The paper reports only single-reference PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, without specifying the sampling or aggregation procedure and without measuring diversity, calibration, likelihood, or uncertainty. On these largely deterministic benchmarks, the claimed multimodal forecasting benefit remains unsupported.

Important technical details are underspecified. The likelihood variance in the ELBO is undefined; the optional rendering loss has no formal definition or weight; the referenced curriculum-learning section is missing (“Section ??”); sequence sampling is not specified precisely; and Stage-1 optimization details are largely omitted.

The decoder predicts rotation and scale parameters, but the manuscript does not explain how unit-quaternion and positive-scale constraints are enforced. A direct L1 loss on quaternions also ignores the q and −q equivalence, potentially making the trajectory objective geometrically inappropriate.

Each Gaussian appears to be forecast independently from its own history, with no explicit spatial or inter-Gaussian interaction mechanism. This limitation is particularly important for coordinated object motion and collisions, yet it is neither discussed nor tested.

Claims that the regularizer enforces C2 smoothness and that the resulting trajectories are physically plausible are overstated. Penalizing finite differences of latent velocities encourages numerical smoothness, but it neither guarantees C2 output trajectories nor imposes physical constraints.

Reproducibility is weak: there is no code or resource statement, parameter count, training/runtime comparison, memory analysis, random-seed variance, confidence intervals, or statistical testing. Several table entries also contradict the prose—for example, the method does not have the lowest LPIPS on every D-NeRF scene.

Overall, the idea is promising but largely combines established components, while the incomplete protocol, missing ablations, and sparse qualitative evidence leave the headline state-of-the-art claim insufficiently substantiated for a top-tier venue. These are substantial rather than marginal omissions.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: continuous-time extrapolation of dynamic 3D scenes rather than interpolation only.
The combination of 3D Gaussian Splatting, trajectory encoding, and latent neural ODE evolution is intuitive and potentially useful, enabling predictions at arbitrary future timestamps.

Reported quantitative results are strong across two datasets. ODE-GS improves average PSNR from 24.02 to 27.01 dB on D-NeRF and from 25.83 to 33.31 dB on NVFI relative to the strongest reported baseline averages.
The evaluation includes the directly relevant GaussianPrediction baseline as well as NeRF- and Gaussian-based alternatives, and reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS per scene.
The two-stage formulation and overall inference pipeline are described clearly, and both deterministic and variational variants are reported.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is incomplete for a top-tier paper. There are no component ablations for the latent ODE, Transformer, second-derivative regularizer, dynamic sequence separation, curriculum, or optional rendering loss, so the source of the reported gains is unclear.

The variational formulation is underspecified and insufficiently validated. Equation 4 omits the expectation over latent samples normally present in an ELBO, the likelihood variance and test-time sampling protocol are unclear, and no uncertainty, calibration, diversity, or multimodal forecasting results support the claimed probabilistic advantage.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are difficult to assess. The paper does not explain how baselines were adapted and tuned for the temporal splits, whether all methods receive equivalent observations, or whether numbers were reproduced under identical settings. The exceptionally large NVFI gains make these details especially important.

Several central claims exceed the evidence. Physical plausibility and temporal smoothness are asserted without trajectory, acceleration, temporal-consistency, or physics-based metrics; arbitrary-time prediction is not evaluated at irregular or intermediate timestamps; and only one qualitative scene is shown.

The method predicts each Gaussian trajectory independently and does not explicitly model interactions among Gaussians or objects. The manuscript does not analyze how this limitation affects collisions, articulated motion, topology changes, or long-horizon stability.

Important technical and implementation details are missing, including parameter constraints for decoded quaternions and scales, the precise trajectory loss and normalization, whether rendering supervision is actually used, forecasting horizons, training cost, inference speed, memory consumption, and Gaussian count scalability.

The novelty is moderate: the main contribution combines established deformable 3DGS, Transformer encoding, and variational latent ODE machinery. Comparisons against simpler trajectory-forecasting controls are needed to show that the ODE formulation itself is essential.

Presentation contains notable inconsistencies and omissions, including an unresolved “Section ??” reference and describing the model as autoregressive even though the stated latent ODE rollout does not feed decoded predictions back as inputs.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: forecasting dynamic 3D scenes beyond the observed temporal window, rather than only interpolating them.

The two-stage design is clear and practically motivated: a frozen dynamic-Gaussian model supplies dense trajectories, while a Transformer and latent ODE perform forecasting without directly extrapolating a timestamp-conditioned deformation field.
Evaluation spans three benchmarks and both synthetic and real-world scenes. The reported gains are particularly strong on many NVFi sequences.

Ablations examine the ODE component, dynamic sampling, regularization, adaptive weighting, and deterministic versus variational formulations. The appendix also provides useful architectural and optimization details.
The continuous-time formulation supports querying intermediate future times and provides an appropriate smoothness bias for scenes with regular motion.
The paper is generally well organized, and the qualitative results and residual visualizations broadly support the quantitative improvements.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the central approach is largely a direct composition of an existing canonical-deformation 3DGS representation, a Transformer encoder, and a standard latent neural ODE, augmented with conventional acceleration penalties.

The main causal comparison is inadequate. The no-ODE baseline is an autoregressive Transformer that feeds predictions back as inputs, introducing accumulated-error and exposure-bias disadvantages absent from the proposed decoder. Strong controlled alternatives such as direct multi-step Transformers, constant-velocity/acceleration predictors, spline extrapolation, recurrent models, and non-ODE continuous-time models are missing.

The evidence does not support the broad claims of stable extrapolation at arbitrary future horizons. Results use one dataset-specific temporal split and aggregate all held-out frames, without quality-versus-horizon curves, substantially longer rollouts, irregular-time tests, or stability analysis outside the tested interval.

Only per-frame appearance metrics are reported. There are no trajectory, temporal-consistency, motion, or physical-plausibility metrics, so the claimed physically plausible and coherent dynamics are not directly established.

Several textual claims overstate the tables. ODE-GS does not consistently outperform the baselines: it is substantially worse on D-NeRF Bouncing Balls, loses some metrics on Trex and multiple HyperNeRF scenes, and performs poorly on NVFi Falling Ball. The stated aggregate percentage improvements are not derived transparently and appear sensitive to how heterogeneous metrics are averaged.

Forecasting is supervised only against pseudo-trajectories produced by the interpolation model, rather than images or ground-truth geometry. This can propagate reconstruction errors and representation-specific artifacts; the paper provides little analysis of this error transfer or whether image-level fine-tuning would help.

Most models are trained separately for each scene, limiting evidence that the approach learns broadly reusable dynamics. The multi-scene study holds out only the simple Whale scene and remains too narrow to substantiate cross-scene generalization.

Important reproducibility and efficiency information is missing, including code availability, exact baseline tuning and checkpoint selection, Gaussian counts, training and inference times, memory consumption, solver evaluation counts, and variability across random seeds.

The representation forecasts each Gaussian trajectory from its own parameter history without an explicit mechanism for inter-Gaussian interactions or object-level constraints. This makes strong performance on collisions, contacts, occlusions, and abrupt coordinated motion theoretically questionable and is consistent with some reported failures.

The formulation leaves technical details unclear, including parameter normalization across position, scale, and quaternion components, enforcement of valid unit quaternions and positive scales, correspondence stability after densification, and how continuous query times are scaled for ODE integration.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and relatively underexplored problem: forecasting renderable dynamic 3D scenes beyond the observed temporal window.
The proposed two-stage pipeline is coherent: a frozen dynamic-GS model supplies trajectories, while a Transformer encoder, latent ODE, and decoder perform continuous-time forecasting.

Evaluation covers synthetic and real-world datasets and reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Several scenes show substantial improvements, particularly Mutant and Standup on D-NeRF and several NVFi object scenes.
The authors include component ablations, per-scene results, a deterministic-versus-variational comparison, qualitative error maps, and a preliminary cross-scene experiment.
The paper is generally readable, and the main limitations involving interpolation quality, abrupt motion, and scene-specific fitting are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited: the central method is a fairly direct composition of an existing deformable-GS representation, a Transformer sequence encoder, and a standard latent neural ODE with smoothness penalties. The paper does not establish a substantial technical advance over these ingredients.

The experimental evidence does not support several broad claims. Smooth trajectories are repeatedly described as physically plausible, but the evaluation contains no physical, geometric, trajectory, or long-horizon stability metrics. Image similarity alone cannot establish physical plausibility or correct motion.

The claim that the method eliminates timestamp dependence and mitigates out-of-distribution extrapolation is overstated. The ODE is still evaluated at requested future times and its latent state is integrated beyond the region encountered during training; this changes the extrapolation mechanism but does not remove distribution shift.

Baseline comparisons are insufficiently documented. The paper does not explain in adequate detail how interpolation-oriented methods were adapted and tuned for each temporal split, omits some baselines from some datasets, reports no repeated trials or uncertainty, and lacks simple but important forecasting controls such as constant-velocity, polynomial/spline, direct non-autoregressive, or matched discrete latent-dynamics baselines.

The key 'without ODE' ablation substitutes an autoregressive Transformer, simultaneously changing continuous versus discrete dynamics and direct versus autoregressive decoding. Its large degradation therefore does not isolate the contribution of the ODE formulation.

The method predicts every Gaussian trajectory independently and provides no explicit spatial interaction mechanism. This is a consequential restriction for collisions, articulated structures, occlusions, and coordinated multi-object motion, yet its effect is neither analyzed nor ablated.

The treatment of Gaussian parameters is technically underspecified. Raw L1 regression is applied jointly to positions, quaternion rotations, and scales, but the paper does not describe quaternion normalization or a sign-invariant/geodesic rotation loss, nor how valid scales are enforced. These omissions raise correctness and reproducibility concerns.

The dynamic-sampling equations appear internally inconsistent: with indices i=1,...,Nc and delta=Tc/(Nc-1), the final context sample extends beyond the stated context endpoint. The main text and implementation details also use Tc and Te ambiguously for both temporal spans and sequence lengths.

Extrapolation performance is not measured as a function of forecast horizon, despite long-horizon behavior being the central motivation. Dataset-specific splits range from 10% to 25%, and selected qualitative results show only isolated timestamps, making stability and degradation beyond the tested interval unclear.

Some empirical summaries are misleading. ODE-GS is not consistently best on HyperNeRF or D-NeRF, and claims formed by averaging percentage changes across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are not statistically or semantically well justified. HyperNeRF scenes are also said to be randomly selected without reporting the selection seed or results on the remaining scenes.

The deterministic single-future formulation does not address the fundamental multimodality of future dynamics. The variational variant performs poorly, but this does not justify presenting the deterministic smooth continuation as the 'most likely' future.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: there is no stated code or model release, no runtime or memory analysis, no number of Gaussians or resulting training-set scale, and insufficient detail on baseline training, sampling frequency, normalization of heterogeneous Gaussian parameters, and scene-specific optimization.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: extrapolating dynamic 3D scenes beyond observed timestamps rather than merely interpolating within the training window.

The two-stage formulation is sensible: a frozen dynamic Gaussian model supplies dense trajectories, while a Transformer and latent neural ODE forecast their continuous-time evolution without directly extrapolating timestamp embeddings.

Evaluation is broad, covering three benchmarks and both synthetic and real-world scenes. The method achieves substantial average improvements, particularly on NVFi, with convincing qualitative residual visualizations.

The paper includes useful ablations of the ODE component, dynamic sampling, regularization, and adaptive weighting. The per-scene results also expose failure cases instead of only reporting aggregate metrics.
The method is clearly motivated, reasonably well described, and accompanied by important implementation and dataset-split details.
weaknesses: The claims of physically plausible motion and stable extrapolation to arbitrary future horizons are stronger than the evidence. Evaluation uses image-quality metrics over fixed, relatively short held-out windows, without physical-consistency metrics, trajectory errors, or performance-versus-horizon curves showing long-rollout stability.

Novelty is moderate: the principal components—canonical Gaussian deformation, Transformer sequence encoding, latent neural ODE evolution, and smoothness regularization—are established techniques. The contribution is primarily their integration and application to dynamic-scene extrapolation.

The comparison against the non-ODE autoregressive Transformer is confounded by autoregressive error accumulation. Stronger controlled alternatives such as direct multi-step prediction, constant-velocity or spline extrapolation, and a continuous-time model without the neural ODE would better isolate the source of the gains.

Performance is not uniformly superior. The method substantially underperforms competitors on D-NeRF Bouncingballs and NVFi Fallingball, is not best on several HyperNeRF metrics, and offers only modest gains on some scenes. Statements such as consistently surpassing the baselines should therefore be qualified.

Most results use a separately trained forecasting model for each scene. The preliminary multi-scene experiment covers one simple held-out scene and generally trails per-scene training, leaving cross-scene generalization and practical forecasting of genuinely novel dynamics insufficiently established.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence is incomplete: there are no multiple-seed results or uncertainty estimates, limited detail about baseline retraining and tuning, and no training time, inference speed, memory consumption, or released-code statement. There are also minor notation ambiguities involving context length versus context span and insufficient discussion of quaternion normalization and scale constraints.
